A Virginia police officer pepper-sprayed a 27-year-old Army lieutenant in uniform while his dog choked in a crate in the back. Less than a minute earlier, with a gun at his window, Caron Nazario had told them, "I'm honestly afraid to get out." One officer answered, "Yeah, you should be."

Nazario, a second lieutenant in the Army Medical Corps, had been pulled over for a temporary plate the officers said they couldn't see, and he had driven slowly for less than a mile to reach a well-lit BP gas station before stopping. The officer who sprayed him, Joe Gutierrez, had already told him he was "fixing to ride the lightning, son," slang for the electric chair.

In the video below, from Gutierrez's own body camera: the gun at his window, Nazario asking "I'm actively serving this country and this is how you're going to treat me?", the spray, and then the lieutenant sitting with both hands raised, saying "My hands are out, please," "My dog is choking," "I'm a lieutenant." And the officer tells him, "You made this way more difficult than it had to be if you just complied."

His lawsuit says they kneed him in the legs, forced him face down and kept hitting him while he lay on the ground in tears. No charges were filed against him.

Gutierrez was fired four months later, after the video went public. In January 2023 a jury gave Nazario $3,685, $2,685 for the assault by Gutierrez and $1,000 against the other officer, Daniel Crocker, for an illegal search, and sided with the officers on everything else. In 2024 an appeals court revived one of his claims against Gutierrez.

A soldier who should have just stepped out of the car, or a man who was right to be afraid?

Re: The new BIS rule

I missed a provision yesterday.

Under the new rule, chip designers in China and other restricted regions can no longer qualify for an exemption through the existing transistor-count verification process unless they have BIS status as an “approved” or “authorized” IC designer. Under the previous rule, a foundry or an outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) provider could verify the transistor count to establish eligibility for an exemption. Now, BIS itself has to decide whether to grant one.

As a result, foundries such as TSMC and Samsung Electronics, as well as OSAT providers such as ASE and Amkor, will need to conduct more thorough background checks on their customers.
